summary: Proposes a standard for gateway-to-gateway procedures that let gateways be mutually suspicious, as a draft inviting comments. This is the Exterior Gateway Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 827 proposes procedures for gateways in separately managed networks to exchange information about reachable networks. It describes how gateways become neighbors, check whether a neighbor is reachable, and request network lists. The memo warns that EGP does not calculate routes and cannot prevent loops in a topology with cycles.

questions: how does egp neighbor acquisition work
subtitle: A draft protocol for gateways to exchange network reachability across autonomous systems.

tldr.problem: A single shared routing algorithm becomes difficult to maintain as gateways and networks grow, so separately managed systems need to exchange reachability information.
tldr.mechanism: EGP has neighbor acquisition, neighbor reachability checks, and polled Network Reachability messages listing networks for which a gateway is an appropriate first hop.
tldr.outcome: RFC 827 is a draft inviting comments and is updated by RFC 904. It is not a routing algorithm and assumes autonomous systems form a tree without cycles.

today: RFC 827 describes itself as a draft inviting comments, and the unit metadata gives no formal status. It is updated by RFC 904.

sections.title: Why Gateways Need EGP
sections.content:
The RFC argues that one common routing algorithm becomes costly and inflexible as a network grows and includes different gateway systems. It proposes autonomous systems: groups of relatively similar gateways that use their own internal routing methods.

EGP lets gateways in different systems exchange information about networks each can reach. The protocol is a polling protocol, so each gateway can control how often it sends and receives reachability information. Autonomous system identifiers are 16 bits; zero means no identifier is present.
sections.plainLanguage: Each autonomous system can use its own internal routing method. EGP lets neighboring systems exchange limited information about which networks they can reach.

sections.title: Acquiring a Neighbor
sections.content:
Before two gateways exchange reachability information, they use the Neighbor Acquisition Protocol. One gateway sends a request and repeats it until a reply arrives. The other gateway may refuse, or reply and send its own request. They become direct neighbors after each has sent a request and received the matching reply.

A gateway can end the relationship with a Neighbor Cease message, which the other gateway acknowledges. The RFC does not specify how a gateway first decides which other gateway it should approach.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways exchange requests and replies before they begin sharing network information. Either gateway can later end the relationship with a cease message.

sections.title: Checking Neighbor Reachability
sections.content:
Direct neighbors use Hello and I Heard You messages to check reachability. A gateway should reply to a Hello immediately, within a few seconds. The RFC leaves the exact failure-detection algorithm and its parameters to implementers, since they depend on the neighbor and connecting network.

A gateway can also report that it considers the other reachable or unreachable. An unreachable gateway remains a neighbor for a time and may become reachable again without repeating acquisition. If it remains unreachable for an extremely long time, such as an hour, the gateway should stop treating it as a neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors exchange short messages to check whether they can still communicate. The RFC leaves the precise threshold for declaring a neighbor unreachable to the gateway designers.

sections.title: Network Reachability Information
sections.content:
A Network Reachability (NR) message lists networks for which its sender is an appropriate first hop. Each listed network has a one-byte distance value chosen according to the sender's autonomous-system metric. A value of 255 means unreachable; all other values mean reachable.

If a network is absent from one NR message, it remains reachable in the receiver's view. If it is absent from two successive messages, the receiver treats it as no longer reachable. An NR message can also describe other gateways on the shared network, allowing a receiver to learn about indirect neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: An NR message lists the networks a gateway can serve as a first hop. A network omitted twice in a row is treated as unreachable.

sections.title: Polling and EGP Limitations
sections.content:
An NR Poll asks a direct, reachable neighbor for an NR message. A gateway may not poll another more often than once per minute, and it should receive a reply within several seconds. Between polls, the neighbor may send one unsolicited NR message to report a change.

The RFC describes stub gateways that connect local networks to core gateways. It also states important limits: EGP does not provide a routing algorithm or enough information for general hierarchical routing. Its topology assumption is a tree without cycles; with cycles, EGP cannot prevent routing loops. False reachability information can also cause traffic to be lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways request network lists periodically and can send one update between requests. EGP exchanges information but leaves route calculation to another algorithm, and its design cannot handle cyclic autonomous-system topologies safely.
